title: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
desc: Treats verification, confidentiality and security as institution-wide duties because fluent outputs may be false or contextually wrong.

kps.k: Courts increasingly frame AI as supervised assistance, not a transfer of judicial authority.
kps.d: The cluster’s central proposition is that AI may support research, summarisation, drafting, translation, scheduling and case administration, but judges must retain independent analysis, direct engagement with evidence and responsibility for decisions. This boundary reflects concerns about legitimacy, contestability, discretion and contextual judgment, not only model accuracy. A minority view predicts that cost, speed and improving reliability will normalise machine-informed or machine-directed routine adjudication; even that view generally preserves human final appeals, informed consent or legislative safeguards.

qs.q: Human oversight and decision-making: Judges and magistrates should not delegate               any part of their mandate or rely exclusively on AI systems to adopt decisions or auto-               mate entire processes that may negatively impact the rights of individuals or communities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: AI tools may assist, but they cannot replace direct judicial engagement with evidence.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Verification remains the operative safeguard because fluent output can be false, incomplete, outdated, biased or jurisdictionally wrong.
kps.d: Court policies and professional guidance consistently assign humans the work of checking AI output before reliance. They commonly require primary-source confirmation of authorities, factual and jurisdictional review, proofreading, adaptation to the case and scrutiny for bias. Fabricated-citation incidents, inaccurate judicial materials and judges’ reported experiences provide practical evidence of the risk, but they do not establish a general model error rate. Grounding, legal-specific databases, citations and audit logs may make review easier or reduce hallucination risk; none eliminates the verification duty. Verification can also erase expected time savings, especially in legal research.

qs.q: VERIFICATION REQUIREMENT  7.1 Content produced using AI must be verified with meaningful human control.
qs.a: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Those who use artificial intelligence to conduct legal research notwithstanding these            risks have a professional duty therefore to check the accuracy of such research by            reference to authoritative sources, before using it in the course of their professional            work (to advise clients or before a court, for example).
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: AI use leaves existing professional and procedural responsibility with lawyers, litigants and institutional leaders.
kps.d: The materials generally treat competence, diligence, candour, confidentiality, supervision and filing-accuracy duties as technology-neutral. Lawyers remain responsible for work performed personally, by staff or with AI; court users likewise remain responsible for submitted documents. Consequences may include costs, sanctions, struck filings, disciplinary referral or contempt, depending on the governing rule and misconduct. A key disagreement concerns sufficiency: some sources say existing rules such as filing certifications and competence duties already provide robust governance, while others argue that recurring misuse shows that guidance alone is inadequate and that managing partners, chambers heads, regulators and courts must implement effective training, controls and enforcement.

qs.q: The court agreed that existing court rules that require lawyers to certify the accuracy of court filings were sufficient to encompass AI.
qs.a: GenAI Trends in the Legal Profession in 2024 · Law firms · 2024

qs.q: In those circumstances, practical and effective measures must now be taken by those            within the legal profession with individual leadership responsibilities (such as heads of            chambers and managing partners) and by those with the responsibility for regulating            the provision of legal services.
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Governance must cover the full institutional lifecycle, not merely individual prompting.
kps.d: The governance model combines multidisciplinary oversight, named accountability, approved-tool lists, staff and user participation, data governance, procurement controls, pilots, recurrent testing, impact assessment, auditability and stopping rules. Courts should begin with operational problems and demonstrable needs rather than technological enthusiasm, define which tasks remain human, and reassess interim policies as tools and law evolve. Brazilian experience illustrates the risks of fragmented, opaque and rapidly proliferating projects, while state-court examples illustrate approval-based and guideline-based approaches. These are governance examples and recommendations, not proof of improved court outcomes.

qs.q: While specific tasks may vary depending on the organization, the AI governance group or committee typically develops an understanding of the impact of AI, sets a strategic direction for the use of AI, helps to establish polices, monitors compliance, authorizes AI projects, and addresses risks, such as those related to bias, transparency, privacy, and accountability.
qs.a: AI Readiness for the State Courts: A Guide for Courts · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Conduct algorithmic audits and impact                          same vein, as recommended by the Report         evaluations after deploying AI systems.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Confidentiality and security controls depend on the tool, data and deployment environment.
kps.d: Public or externally hosted tools may retain prompts, reuse data for training or expose sensitive information. Policies therefore restrict confidential, privileged, personally identifiable, health and case-related data; some go further by prohibiting even public court filings in nonprivate models. Recommended controls include approved private or enterprise systems, zero retention, organisational authentication, access controls, redaction, contractual review, secure work devices and prompt/output logging. Closed systems can reduce risk but do not remove the need to inspect vendor terms, settings, provenance and cybersecurity. Claims that privilege will necessarily be lost remain concerns rather than settled legal consequences in the supplied material.

qs.q: No user may input into any generative AI program that does not operate on a private model —      by writing a prompt, uploading a document or file, or otherwise — any information that is      confidential, private, or privileged, or includes personally identifiable information or      protected health information, or is otherwise inappropriate for public release.
qs.a: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (New York State Unified Court System) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: 6.9 For closed AI tools:  (a) If Court users input private, confidential or sensitive information into closed AI tools they need to exercise caution and satisfy themselves by reviewing the contractual terms or privacy and confidentiality settings that the information they input will be kept within a secure environment.
qs.a: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Disclosure rules remain contested and jurisdiction-specific.
kps.d: Some courts require disclosure whenever AI directly generates filed content, certification that citations are authentic, or identification of AI’s role in expert evidence. Others require disclosure only when context, provenance, evidential weight, ethics or local rules make it material; England and Wales states that responsible use ordinarily need not be disclosed. The dispute turns partly on whether disclosure promotes transparency and equal treatment or imposes confusing, technology-specific burdens already covered by ordinary accuracy duties. Disclosure does not itself establish reliability, so it supplements rather than replaces verification.

qs.q: To ensure that the Court understands the role AI has played in the preparation of materials for the purpose of litigation, and submitted to the Court by or on behalf of a party or intervener, such materials must include the Declaration whenever they contain content created or generated directly by AI.
qs.a: Notice to the Parties and the Profession — The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings (amended) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Provided AI is used responsibly, there is no reason why a legal representative ought to refer to its use, but this is dependent upon context.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Efficiency and access-to-justice benefits are plausible but uneven, task-dependent and incompletely demonstrated.
kps.d: Sources identify potential gains from court administration, transcription, translation, document processing, legal information and assistance for self-represented litigants. Evidence includes reported operational examples, such as increased case processing with Argentina’s Prometea, and surveys showing meaningful judicial adoption alongside limited training. Most broader claims about backlog reduction, lower costs and improved access remain anticipated benefits rather than measured outcomes. Important countervailing risks include digital exclusion, unaffordable secure systems, unreliable advice, excessive AI-assisted filings and the possibility that greater access to court does not improve substantive access to justice. Practical proposals therefore favour bounded internal pilots before direct-to-client deployment, human escalation and equivalent offline alternatives.

qs.q: 44% are actively using them for tasks including summarizing texts, writing emails, drafting legal documents and conducting legal research.
qs.a: Global Judges' Initiative: Survey on the Use of AI Systems by Judicial Operators · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: The concern is that litigants might have more access to the court, but not access to justice, if such filings overwhelm the system.
qs.a: Judicial Use of Generative AI: Lessons Learned · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: High-stakes adjudication and evidence demand stronger safeguards than routine administrative uses.
kps.d: The materials apply the greatest caution to bail, sentencing, recidivism, liberty, witness and expert evidence, and systems that influence substantive legal outcomes. These uses raise due-process, bias, explainability, authenticity and contestability concerns. Deepfakes and hidden prompt instructions broaden the issue from inaccurate text to manipulation of evidence and court systems. Proposed responses include human gatekeeping, provenance records, forensic verification, opportunities to challenge AI-influenced outputs and suspension or decommissioning where serious harm or rights violations emerge. Some commentators argue that empirical comparisons could justify more predictive AI if it proves more accurate than humans, but the supplied material does not establish that premise.

qs.q: In criminal cases, the use of AI in assessing flight risk, recidivism, and other largely discretionary decisions that involve predictions has generated concerns about due process, reliability, and potential bias.
qs.a: 2023 Year-End Report on the Federal Judiciary · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: Additionally, introduce mechanisms that allow affected parties               to contest and cross-examine any output produced by an AI system that may influence the               outcome of the case at hand, as well as challenge the decisions and hold judicial operators               accountable for their errors.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources generally accept the proposition that court AI should remain assistive, subject to human verification and retained judicial responsibility, and collectively develop it into a broader institutional-governance agenda. Their common reasons are that legal judgment depends on contestability, contextual reasoning and identifiable accountability; fluent outputs may be fabricated or otherwise unreliable; and high-stakes uses implicate fairness, fundamental rights and public confidence. Material extensions include empirical evidence of uneven judicial training and chambers policies, competence-focused education, certification and sanctions, risk-based lifecycle assessment, process-wide governance for online dispute resolution, and Brazilian case studies showing how opacity, decentralised deployment and weak coordination can create accountability gaps. Internal variation concerns emphasis rather than wholesale rejection: some sources foreground the legitimacy limits of machine judgment; others condition greater predictive use on comparative evidence; access-to-justice work stresses bounded legal self-help and user responsibility; and some advocate stronger coordinated controls while others leave courts discretion over implementation. One excerpt contains only headings and cannot establish a position. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of academia or research as a whole.

qs.q: These limitations indicate that GenAI models should be treated as ‘human-in- the-loop’ technologies, where users are responsible for identifying hallucinations and verifying output accuracy.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources accepts the proposition’s core boundary: AI may assist legal and judicial work, but humans must retain judgment, independently verify outputs and remain accountable. Collectively, the sources materially extend the proposition through cross-jurisdictional reporting on implementation and governance. Common reasons include fabricated authorities and other unreliable outputs; the need to protect confidentiality, security and judicial independence; and the limits of efficiency claims that remain prospective or pilot-based. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than direction. The Indian analysis highlights courts moving faster than professional regulators and unresolved confidentiality duties; the Nigerian guidance concentrates on lawyers’ competence, consent and supervision; the federal-courts report describes judiciary-wide controls spanning procurement, security and education but relies on an official account because the underlying guidance was unavailable; the UAE report is more promotional about integration and anticipated economic benefits while still preserving judicial authority and rights safeguards; and the ABA Task Force coverage adds unequal access, deepfake risks and early—but not comprehensive—access-to-justice progress. These sources therefore strengthen lifecycle supervision rather than merely endorsing human oversight, although many claimed efficiency, adoption and economic benefits are predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes.

qs.q: It includes suggestions for AI tool use, procurement, and security, as well as recommendations for specific areas like “confidentiality and security of Judiciary data” and “AI education,” Conrad said.
qs.a: Interim AI guidance for US courts aims for experimentation with guardrails · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: Across this curated set, regulators, courts and professional bodies accept the proposition’s core boundary: AI may assist legal and judicial work, but judges, lawyers and court users retain authority, professional responsibility and the duty to verify outputs before reliance. Their recurring reasons are institutional legitimacy, direct engagement with evidence, contestability, contextual judgment, confidentiality, security, bias and the practical record of fabricated or misleading legal material. Collectively, these sources materially develop the proposition by translating it into lifecycle controls: multidisciplinary governance, named accountability, approved-tool regimes, training, data and procurement safeguards, pilots, impact assessment, auditability, public participation, recurrent review and stopping or decommissioning rules. Some also add evidence that judicial adoption has outpaced organisational guidance and training. Internal variation concerns implementation rather than the core supervised-assistance model: some rely mainly on existing competence, candour and filing duties, while others demand AI-specific institutional controls and enforcement; disclosure ranges from mandatory declarations to context-dependent treatment; and access-to-justice benefits are balanced against digital exclusion, unreliable assistance and increased filing burdens. Material dissent remains: one Vos source predicts routine machine-directed adjudication, while a court-capacity argument questions whether human involvement is inherently necessary. Other Vos material is more qualified, preserving informed consent, legislative safeguards, final human appeals and human development of legal principles. A few excerpts are too limited to classify because they provide only definitions or links.

qs.q: **Absence of Guidance and Training on AI**  There is a significant lack of guidance and training on AI usage is evident, with just 9% of judicial operators reporting that their organizations have issued guidelines or provided AI-related training.
qs.a: Global Judges' Initiative: Survey on the Use of AI Systems by Judicial Operators · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The traditional-law-firm source supports the proposition’s core allocation of responsibility: AI should augment legal professionals rather than displace their judgment, and lawyers remain accountable for the accuracy of AI-assisted filings. Its principal reason is that ordinary professional and procedural duties can remain technology-neutral—AI use does not excuse sanctionable conduct—while new synthetic-media risks require careful authentication. Materially, however, it is less committed than the cluster synthesis to heightened, AI-specific controls: it predicts that improving accuracy may lead courts to rely on existing filing rules rather than special verification requirements. That is a disagreement about regulatory form, not about continued human responsibility. The source also extends the immediate concern from checking generated legal text to authenticating potentially AI-produced client materials, though this is presented as a forecast of an emerging duty rather than an established rule. Because the evidence comes from one curated traditional-practice source, it should not be treated as representative of law firms generally.

qs.q: The court agreed that existing court rules that require lawyers to certify the accuracy of court filings were sufficient to encompass AI.
qs.a: GenAI Trends in the Legal Profession in 2024 · Law firms · 2024

qs.q: The increasing sophistication of deepfake technology in voice, images, and video presents novel issues for courts and lawyers who must authenticate each of these sources.
qs.a: GenAI Trends in the Legal Profession in 2024 · Law firms · 2024

vlens.an: The legal-tech vendor source supports the principal proposition that AI should remain supervised assistance and that humans retain responsibility for checking outputs before reliance. It grounds this position in fluent fabrication risks affecting lawyers, litigants and judges, and in existing procedural and professional duties requiring accurate filings, technological competence and verification against primary authorities. Its emphasis is narrower than the cluster’s full lifecycle-governance model: it concentrates on output verification and individual accountability rather than procurement, institutional oversight, security, auditing or stopping rules. Within that narrower frame, it argues that existing rules already provide robust governance and that legal-specific platforms may reduce risk through curated sources, citation checks and audit trails. These claims do not weaken the core position because the source still treats independent human verification as mandatory. As this facet contains one curated source, it establishes this source’s alignment rather than the prevalence of that view among legal-tech vendors.

qs.q: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 and its state counterparts establish clear certification requirements for court filings, making attorneys personally responsible for verifying all submitted content, regardless of its technological origin.
qs.a: From 'trust but verify' to 'do not trust until verified': How the legal profession is redefining AI accountability · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

elens.an: The 2015–2022 sources accept the proposition’s core boundary: courts may use AI as assistance, but judicial professionals should retain review, contextual judgment and identifiable accountability. They commonly justify that boundary through contestability, institutional legitimacy, fundamental rights, bias risks, transparency and the limits of encodable evidence—not accuracy alone. They also materially develop lifecycle supervision through pre-deployment testing, continuing impact assessment, external scrutiny, public participation and advance workforce-transition planning. There is meaningful variation within this shared direction: one source is strongly sceptical of AI judges and opaque outputs; CEPEJ affirmatively encourages useful, rights-compatible applications while reserving greatest caution for criminal matters; the early-court account favours bounded administrative experimentation but treats benefits as unevaluated; and the ethics analysis leaves open greater predictive use if empirical research establishes superior accuracy, without endorsing transfer of final authority. These earlier materials do not substantially address later generative-AI concerns such as fabricated output verification, confidentiality, security or disclosure rules. Because the corpus is curated, these alignments indicate the selected sources’ arguments rather than the prevalence of those views in the period.

qs.q: ■ Professionals in the justice system should, at any moment, be able to review judicial decisions and the data used to produce a result and continue not to be necessarily bound by it in the light of the specific features of that particular case.
qs.a: European Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems and their Environment · Regulators & courts · 2018

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition and, taken together, materially develop it. Their common boundary is that AI may assist legal research, drafting, administration and access-to-justice functions, but judges and lawyers retain judgment, verification and accountability. The recurring reasons are fabricated or contextually wrong output, bias and due-process risks, confidentiality and security concerns, the need for contestable judicial reasoning, and the continuing force of technology-neutral professional and procedural duties. Several sources extend this into concrete lifecycle governance: pre-deployment impact assessment, pilots or sandboxes, recurrent review, multidisciplinary taskforces, procurement and data controls, education, explainability and institutional leadership. UNESCO adds survey evidence that reported judicial use was substantially ahead of organisational guidance and training, strengthening the case for institution-wide controls. Material variation concerns means rather than the core proposition: some favour AI-specific disclosure or certification, while others consider ordinary filing-accuracy rules sufficient; some leave governance responses to individual courts, while COSCA and the Canadian Judicial Council prescribe fuller institutional frameworks. Access-to-justice and efficiency gains are generally presented as plausible or illustrated by limited operational examples, not established across court systems. Forecasts also vary over whether routine adjudication may become more automated, but the sources remain cautious about replacing judicial authority. The Singapore excerpt is substantively unclear because it supplies scope and definitions without supervisory requirements. Because this is a curated selection, these alignments and variations should not be read as representative prevalence among jurisdictions or professional bodies.

qs.q: Impact assessments should be done on a continual basis to keep up with the dynamic development cycle of AI tools and include projected long-term impacts.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: **Absence of Guidance and Training on AI**  There is a significant lack of guidance and training on AI usage is evident, with just 9% of judicial operators reporting that their organizations have issued guidelines or provided AI-related training.
qs.a: Global Judges' Initiative: Survey on the Use of AI Systems by Judicial Operators · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an:
The 2025 material collectively builds on the proposition that court AI requires lifecycle supervision. The sources generally accept AI as supervised assistance rather than a transfer of judicial authority, then develop that principle into operational arrangements for adoption at scale: multidisciplinary governance bodies, named lifecycle accountability, approved-tool controls, mandatory training, data governance, secure deployment, pre-adoption assessment, piloting, recurrent testing, audit trails, impact evaluation, stakeholder participation and suspension or decommissioning where harms emerge. Common reasons include the risk that fluent output is fabricated, outdated, biased or contextually wrong; the non-delegable character of judicial judgment; confidentiality and cybersecurity exposure; and the need to preserve due process, contestability, judicial independence and public confidence.

Material variation concerns how prescriptive and institution-wide these safeguards should be. New York and some judicial policies impose mandatory approval, training, data restrictions and verification, whereas professional guidance from the CCBE and Bar Council is broader or non-binding. England and Wales and the federal Judiciary favour context-sensitive disclosure rather than universal disclosure, while UNESCO and some academic proposals favour more extensive transparency, auditability and contestability. Sources also differ in adoption ambition: the UAE account and Indian white paper envisage integrated or extensive assistive systems, while Vos is more cautious about machine adjudication and Brazilian case studies stress opacity, fragmented deployment and uncertain enforcement. Some sources extend governance beyond court operations to access to justice, digital inclusion, training-data provenance, labour and embedded values. The principal qualification is evidential: most claimed efficiency, backlog and access-to-justice gains are prospective, illustrative or reported institutional examples rather than measured outcomes. Two directory or table-of-contents excerpts are substantively unclear. No supplied 2025 source clearly rejects the proposition, but this is a curated corpus and the pattern should not be treated as representative prevalence.

qs.q: Personnel responsible for different phases of the AI system                lifecycle are identified and held accountable for the outcomes of the AI solutions.
qs.a: AI Readiness for the State Courts: A Guide for Courts · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core boundary—AI may assist legal and judicial work, but humans retain responsibility, verify outputs and protect confidential information—and materially develop it into a more operational governance model. Guidance from Singapore, Victoria, India and New York specifies risk-proportionate review, approved-tool classifications, secure deployment, training, pilots, audit trails, mandatory sign-off and escalation. Survey and interview evidence adds that adoption and chambers policies remain uneven, training is often limited, judges report fabricated authorities, and verification can erase expected research efficiencies. Material variation concerns both governance sufficiency and judicial authority: some sources regard existing professional and procedural duties as adequate, while others call for AI-specific institutional controls; Vos predicts machine-informed or machine-directed routine adjudication, and capacity-focused commentary questions whether judging must remain human. Other sources redirect attention toward individual-user responsibility or technology-mediated access to justice. These dissenting and alternative framings do not displace the period’s overall development of supervised, lifecycle-based adoption, but they show that the boundary between copilot assistance and machine decision-making remains contested. Because the corpus is curated, this assessment characterises the supplied arguments rather than the prevalence of views among judges, courts or legal professionals generally.

qs.q: But there was unanimous consensus among the judges that, regardless of how they are using GenAI, judges must always remain “the deciders” who determine the ultimate outcome of any legal decision before them.
